ana_01.title: Census scope: 5,726 launches, 1957-2018, 94% success
ana_01.claim: The dataset is a complete census, not a sample: 5,726 orbital launch attempts from the first ever (Sputnik, 1957) through October 2018, drawn from Jonathan McDowell's JSR catalog. It spans 62 calendar years, 17 launching-state codes and 366 distinct vehicle types. Overall 5,384 attempts succeeded and 342 failed — a 94.0% all-era success rate. By operator type, 4,776 launches were by state programs, 880 by established 'private' commercial providers and 70 by venture 'startups'. One launch_date typo (2918-10-11) was corrected to 2018-10-11 (the Soyuz MS-10 abort).
ana_01.code:
# Census of orbital launch attempts 1957-2018 (outcome + agency_type counts from launches.csv).
outcomes = {'Success (O)': 5384, 'Failure (F)': 342}
total = sum(outcomes.values())
print(f'orbital launch attempts (1957-2018): {total}')
print(f"successes {outcomes['Success (O)']}  failures {outcomes['Failure (F)']}")
print(f'overall success rate: {100*outcomes["Success (O)"]/total:.1f}%')
print('agency_type split:', {'state': 4776, 'private': 880, 'startup': 70})
ana_01.expected_output:
orbital launch attempts (1957-2018): 5726
successes 5384  failures 342
overall success rate: 94.0%
agency_type split: {'state': 4776, 'private': 880, 'startup': 70}

data_preview.description: Census scope: launches by outcome

ana_02.title: Global launches per year (the 'how much' is roughly flat)
ana_02.claim: Launch volume rose steeply through the early 1960s, then held a Cold-War cruising altitude of roughly 100-140 launches a year from the mid-1960s to 1990 (single-year peak: 139 in 1967). After the Soviet collapse it fell to a 2001-2009 trough near 53-77 a year, before a partial recovery in the 2010s. 2018 shows 80, but this is a PARTIAL year — the data ends in October 2018; the true full-year total was 114 (det_11). The headline 'how much' line is essentially flat-to-down across six decades: the real change is in WHO launches, not how much gets launched.
ana_02.expected_output:
peak year: 1967 with 139 launches
2018 (PARTIAL, Jan-Oct): 80  (external full-year total: 114)

It carries the whole arc at a glance — a US/USSR duel through the early 1960s, Soviet dominance from the 1970s, the post-1991 Soviet/Russian collapse, Europe's steady commercial rise from the mid-1980s, and China climbing from its first launch (1970) to overtake everyone in (partial) 2018: USSR/Russia 10, USA 27, China 28. 2018 is partial (Jan-Oct), so its bars are undercounts of the full year.

ana_04.title: Cumulative ledger: the Cold-War duopoly is still 85% of all launches
ana_04.claim: Over the full era the Cold-War duopoly still dominates the cumulative ledger: USSR/Russia 3,178 launches (55.5% of every orbital launch ever) and the USA 1,716 (30.0%) together account for 85.5% of all launches in history. Europe (307, 5.4%) narrowly leads China (302, 5.3%) on the all-time count — but China's launches are overwhelmingly recent. Japan (115, 2.0%), India (65, 1.1%) and all others combined (43, 0.8%) form the tail. The cumulative picture is the OLD world; the per-year picture (ana_03) is the new one.
ana_04.code:
# Cumulative launches by country, all era 1957-2018 (SU+RU merged into USSR/Russia).
cum = {'USSR/Russia':3178,'USA':1716,'Europe':307,'China':302,'Japan':115,'India':65,'Other':43}
total = sum(cum.values())
for c,n in sorted(cum.items(), key=lambda x:-x[1]):
    print(f'{c:12} {n:5} ({100*n/total:.1f}%)')
old = 100*(cum['USSR/Russia']+cum['USA'])/total
print(f'old-world (USSR/Russia + USA): {old:.1f}%')
ana_04.expected_output:

Japan          115 (2.0%)

old-world (USSR/Russia + USA): 85.5%

ana_06.title: National share of launches by decade (no bloc holds a majority by 2010s)
ana_06.claim: Reframed as shares of the global total, the pluralization is stark. The USSR/Russia share runs 21%->44%->74%->80%->48%->37%->28% across the 1950s-2010s; the US share falls from 79% (1950s) to a low of 13% (1980s, the Soviet peak) and recovers to 26% (2010s); China rises from ~0 to 23% by the 2010s; Europe peaks near 13% (2000s). For the first time since the 1950s, no single bloc holds a majority of launches in the 2010s.

ana_07.title: Concentration: the superpower duopoly's share fell from ~99% to 54%
ana_07.claim: The single cleanest measure of 'a duel became a crowd': the two Cold-War superpowers' combined share of global launches falls from 100% (1950s) and ~99% (1960s) to 93.5% (1980s), 81.2% (1990s), 70.5% (2000s) and just 54.5% in the 2010s. A 7-group Herfindahl index drops in step from ~6,600 toward ~2,200. The number of countries launching in a decade rose from 2 to 7. The US never collapsed — it lost its two-way monopoly as the field filled in around it.
ana_07.expected_output:
1960s: US + USSR/Russia = 98.9% of launches
2010s: US + USSR/Russia = 54.5% of launches

ana_08.title: Two commercialization waves: Arianespace (1984) then startups (2006)
ana_08.claim: A new KIND of actor appears late. 'Startup' launches (almost all SpaceX, plus Rocket Lab) first appear in 2006 and reach 8.8% of all launches in the 2010s. The older 'private' commercial category (led by Arianespace from 1984) peaked earlier — 30.9% of launches in the 1990s and 46.9% in the 2000s — then fell to 36.3% in the 2010s as STATE launches rebounded (China). So commercialization is not one monotonic trend: an Arianespace-style commercial wave (1984-2000s) was followed by a venture-startup wave (2006-), even as a parallel new state surge (China) ran alongside. 'Private' and 'startup' are genuinely different vintages of actor.

ana_09.title: Reliability matured to a 95-97% plateau
ana_09.claim: Launch reliability matured fast then plateaued high: the success rate rose from 46.2% in the experimental 1950s to 87.0% (1960s), 94.9% (1970s) and a 97.1% peak in the 1980s, holding at 95-97% ever since (96.3% in the 2010s). The all-era rate is 94.0%, dragged down only by the high-failure pioneering years. Modern orbital launch is a high-reliability activity (det_13).

ana_10.title: Every major power launches at 89-96%; new contenders match incumbents
ana_10.claim: Every major launching power clusters in a tight, high-reliability band: Europe 95.8%, China 95.7%, USSR/Russia 95.2%, USA 92.4%, Japan 92.2%, India 89.2%. Only the small 'Other' bucket (early Israeli, Iranian, Brazilian and North-Korean and other experimental programs) sits low at 65.1%, on just 43 attempts. The crucial point against any 'cutting corners' read: the new contenders are NOT trading reliability for entry — China's 95.7% matches the incumbents exactly.

ana_19.title: VALIDATION: 'China overtakes 2018' holds at partial, annualized AND full-year
ana_19.claim: Validation of the 'China overtakes' headline, stated at the right level. WHAT IS VALIDATED: the per-year COUNT crossover. China leads at three independent granularities — (a) the dataset's own partial Jan-Oct 2018 window (China 28 > USA 27 > Russia 10); (b) a naive linear annualization of that window (x12/10: China ~33.6, USA ~32.4 — China still ahead); (c) external full-year 2018 records that are independent of this dataset (China 39, USA 34, Russia 20). Across all 62 years, China is the single largest launcher in EXACTLY ONE year — 2018 — so this is a genuine first crossover, not a recurring fluke. COMPARABILITY: the external 39/34/20 are full-calendar-year counts from year-end launch logs (Wikipedia '2018 in spaceflight'); this dataset is a Jan-Oct partial census from McDowell's JSR — different timepoints, not a contradiction. LEVEL GAP: this validates a per-year ranking; the broader thesis ('the field pluralized / a duel became a crowd') is a structural claim validated separately by the concentration metric (ana_07), not by the 2018 count alone. WHAT WOULD FALSIFY IT: if full-year 2018 US launches had exceeded China's (they did not), or if China had led by count in any earlier year (it had not).
ana_19.expected_output:
country       partial  naive_annualized  external_full_year
China            28             33.6                 39
USA              27             32.4                 34
USSR/Russia      10             12.0                 20

det_01.title: Origin: Economist Graphic Detail article + JSR database
det_01.claim: This dataset is the data behind The Economist's Graphic Detail piece 'The space race is dominated by new contenders' (published online 2018-10-18; the dataset folder is dated 2018-10-20). The Economist publishes the data and code behind its Graphic Detail charts in a public GitHub repository. The principal source is Jonathan McDowell's JSR Launch Vehicle Database; the agencies table is credited jointly to McDowell and The Economist. Two CSVs ship with it: launches.csv (one row per orbital launch attempt) and agencies.csv (one row per launch-provider organization/phase). The article's headline IS the thesis the data is meant to support — that the set of actors launching into orbit has broadened beyond the original superpowers.

det_02.title: The source: Jonathan McDowell & the JSR Launch Vehicle Database
det_02.claim: The numbers come from Jonathan McDowell, an astrophysicist at the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics who has maintained 'Jonathan's Space Report' (JSR) and an associated set of launch catalogs since the 1980s. The JSR Launch Vehicle Database aims to list every type of space launch vehicle, suborbital and orbital, and his master launch log is widely treated as the most complete public record of orbital launch attempts, with launch times to the second where available. It is a reference-grade, hand-curated catalog rather than an official government dataset — which matters for the analyst because edge cases (a launch's success/failure status, an agency's nationality, an org's start/stop dates) reflect McDowell's adjudication. Provenance note: the dataset README links to the LVDB at http://www.planet4589.org/space/lvdb/index.html, which now returns HTTP 404; McDowell reorganized the site (the catalog now lives under planet4589.org/space/gcat and the master launch log at planet4589.org/space/log/launch.html). The data itself is unaffected — only the README's link rotted.

det_03.title: Sputnik 1957 — why the data starts where it does
det_03.claim: The dataset opens on 1957-10-04, the day the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the world's first artificial satellite. Sputnik's success was a shock in the United States, triggering the 'Sputnik crisis' and, the following year, the creation of NASA. That single launch is the origin of both the 'space race' framing the article uses and of orbital launch record-keeping itself — so the dataset's first row is, in effect, the first orbital launch in history. Every count in this data is therefore a complete, not sampled, census of the orbital era from its very first day.

det_04.title: Why the USSR dwarfs everyone: Kosmos + the Soyuz/R-7 workhorse
det_04.claim: The single biggest fact in the raw counts — the USSR has more launches (2,444) than any other state, and the most-launched vehicles in the data are all Soviet (Soyuz-U at 632, Kosmos 11K65M at 445, Voskhod and Molniya variants) — has a concrete external explanation. First, the 'Kosmos' (Cosmos) label was a catch-all designation covering almost all Soviet/Russian military satellites plus many scientific and test payloads; 2,548 Kosmos-numbered satellites had been launched by January 2021. Many were short-lived military reconnaissance, communications, and early-warning craft that had to be replaced frequently, driving a high launch cadence. Second, the Soviet/Russian launch fleet was built on the R-7 'Semyorka' — the world's first ICBM (first flight 1957, Korolev's design bureau) — whose Soyuz derivatives became the most-launched orbital rocket family in history (over 2,000 launches, a success rate above 97%). So the Soviet dominance in this dataset is a story of cheap, reliable, mass-produced hardware flown very often, not of a few spectacular missions.

det_05.title: The 1990s dip: the post-Soviet collapse
det_05.claim: The data shows global launch volume falling from its 1980s peak (about 1,191 launches in the 1980s) to roughly 889 in the 1990s and 650 in the 2000s, with the Soviet 'SU' code vanishing after 1991 and a smaller Russian 'RU' program taking its place. The external cause is the collapse of the Soviet Union. Russian space funding was cut by about 80% through the 1990s — from a 1989 peak of 6.9 billion rubles (about 1.5% of GDP) down to roughly 0.23% of the budget by the mid-1990s — and the workforce shrank from about 400,000 (1987) toward 100,000 by the late-1990s crisis. The flagship Buran shuttle was cancelled in 1993, and the main launch site, Baikonur, ended up in newly independent Kazakhstan. This is why the dataset's middle period sags: the launch leader of the Cold War nearly stopped flying.

det_06.title: The rise of China: Long March, Dong Fang Hong, Shenzhou
det_06.claim: China is the clearest 'new contender'. In the data its launches climb from a handful in the 1970s (13) to 39 in the 1990s, 64 in the 2000s and 171 in the 2010s, and 287 of its 302 launches are Long March ('Chang Zheng', CZ) rockets. The history: under the 'Two Bombs, One Satellite' program China launched its first satellite, Dong Fang Hong 1, on a Long March 1 on 1970-04-24, becoming the fifth nation to reach orbit independently. The Long March family is built by the China Academy of Launch Vehicle Technology (CALT) under the state giant CASC. China became the third nation to fly humans to orbit on its own with Shenzhou 5 on 2003-10-15, and the Long March family ran 75 consecutive successful launches from October 1996 to April 2009. By the dataset's end China is no longer a minor player but a launch superpower in the making.

det_07.title: The headline moment: China out-launched everyone in 2018
det_07.claim: The event that makes 2018 the right vantage point — and gives the article its title — is that 2018 became the first year in which more rockets reached orbit from China than from any other country. Over the full year China conducted 39 orbital launches (38 successes, 1 failure) versus 34 for the United States and 20 for Russia, and the global total hit 114 — the first time more than 100 orbital launches were performed in a single year since 1990, a 25% jump on 2017's 91. (Important caveat for the analyst: this dataset was compiled around the article's October 2018 publication, so it contains only a partial 2018 — see det_11 — and shows China 28 vs US 27 in its truncated window; the full-year figures above come from external year-end records.) The shift is not that the US declined but that a third pole emerged.

det_08.title: The 'startup' contender: SpaceX and reusability
det_08.claim: The data carries a rare third agency_type beyond 'state' and 'private': 'startup', and in this dataset it is almost entirely SpaceX (62 Falcon 9 + 5 Falcon 1 + 1 Falcon Heavy = 68 rows; Rocket Lab supplies the rest). SpaceX was founded in 2002. After three failures that nearly bankrupted it, Falcon 1 reached orbit on 2008-09-28, the first privately developed, fully liquid-fueled rocket to do so. Falcon 9 first flew on 2010-06-04; in December 2015 SpaceX landed a Falcon 9 first stage back on the ground, the breakthrough toward reusability; and the Falcon Heavy first flew on 2018-02-06 — landing its two side boosters simultaneously — squarely inside this dataset's window. The 'startup' label is the data's way of marking a genuinely new kind of actor: a venture-funded private firm driving launch costs down through reuse, distinct from the older state-contractor 'private' providers.

det_09.title: The smallsat new entrant: Rocket Lab Electron
det_09.claim: The other 'startup' in the data is Rocket Lab, whose Electron rocket appears with its first orbital flights. Electron reached orbit on 2018-01-21, deploying three CubeSats, and flew its first commercial mission on 2018-11-11. Electron is a dedicated small-satellite launcher — built to carry 200-300 kg to a Sun-synchronous orbit — and it opened up frequent, dedicated access to orbit for small-satellite operators, a segment previously stuck hitching rides as secondary payloads. Its presence (alongside SpaceX) signals a second axis of the 'new contenders' story that runs orthogonal to the country story: not just new nations, but a new class of small, commercial, high-cadence launch providers emerging right at the dataset's edge.

det_10.title: The first commercial wave: Arianespace
det_10.claim: Long before SpaceX, the 'private' agency_type in this data was led by Europe. Arianespace, founded on 1980-03-26, was the world's first commercial launch-service provider, created to commercialize the European Space Agency's Ariane rockets. In the dataset, Arianespace (agency code 'AE', state 'F' for France/Europe) accounts for 258 launches — the largest single 'private' provider before the SpaceX era, and its Ariane 5 is among the most-flown vehicles in the data. This matters for interpreting the agency_type field: 'private' is not new — it dates to 1980 and grew steadily through the 1990s-2000s — whereas 'startup' is the genuinely recent category. An analyst tracking 'commercialization' should distinguish the older Arianespace-style commercial providers from the newer venture-backed startups.

det_11.title: CAVEAT: 2018 is a partial year in this dataset
det_11.claim: The most important analytical caveat: this dataset is truncated at the article's publication. The latest real launch dates are in October 2018, and the 2018 rows total only 80 launches, with monthly counts thinning out after August. By contrast, external year-end records show 114 orbital launches globally in 2018. So 2018 in this data is roughly a 9-to-10-month snapshot, not a full year. Any chart that compares 2018 head-to-head with prior full years will understate 2018 and can produce a misleading 'decline'. The fix is to either label 2018 as partial, annualize it, or stop the continuous trend at 2017 and mark 2018 separately. The 'China overtakes' story still holds (it holds even more strongly at full-year), but the magnitude must be read with the truncation in mind.

det_12.title: CAVEAT: state codes, the 1991 break, and a data typo
det_12.claim: Three structural caveats for the analyst, all visible in the raw fields. (1) The Soviet/Russian discontinuity: launches before 1991 carry state_code 'SU' and after carry 'RU' (and military org codes like RVSN/UNKS give way to VKSR). To draw one continuous 'USSR -> Russia' line, SU and RU must be merged; treating them as two separate countries hides that the same program is the through-line of the whole dataset. (2) 'F' denotes France/Europe and is effectively the ESA/Arianespace bloc (with separate 'I-ESA' / 'I-ELDO' codes for multinational European bodies) — it is European launch activity, not just French. (3) There is at least one date typo: a row with launch_year 2018 carries launch_date '2918-10-11' (a mistyped '2918' for '2018'); parse on launch_year, not raw launch_date, or clean that value. Also note agencies.csv's pre-computed 'count' column can differ slightly from a fresh row-count of launches.csv (e.g. SpaceX shows 65 in agencies.csv vs 68 launch rows) because the two were tallied at slightly different cutoffs — prefer recomputing from launches.csv for consistency.

det_13.title: BENCHMARK: orbital launch is now highly reliable
det_13.claim: For any success/failure analysis, the relevant benchmark is that mature orbital launch is now a high-reliability activity. In this dataset every major launching state sits between roughly 89% and 98% success (e.g. France/Europe ~98%, Russia ~97%, USSR ~95%, China ~96%, US ~92%, India ~89%), and overall 5,384 of 5,726 attempts succeeded (~94%). Externally this is corroborated: the Soyuz/R-7 family exceeds 97% success across 2,000+ flights, and CSIS reports China's Long March at a 95.3% success rate — comparable to the US Delta (95.5%) and Soyuz (97.2%). So the 'new contenders' are not cutting corners on reliability; China and the commercial entrants are competitive with the incumbents on this dimension. Treat sub-90% or early-program failure clusters (e.g. SpaceX's three early Falcon 1 failures) as the exceptions that prove a high baseline, not the norm.

det_14.title: Why it matters: launch access is national power and a $1tn market
det_14.claim: Why a general reader should care: who can launch, and how cheaply, decides who controls the satellites that run modern life — communications, navigation (GPS, GLONASS, BeiDou), Earth observation, and military reconnaissance and early warning. Indigenous launch capability is held by only a handful of nations and is treated as a marker of top-tier technological and strategic power; everyone else depends on those few providers. The economics are large and growing: CSIS cites estimates that the global space economy grows from about $350 billion (2016) toward more than $1 trillion by 2040, with reusable rockets sharply cutting launch costs. Against that backdrop, China executed 207 launches in 2010-2019 — more than in the prior four decades combined — narrowing the gap with the US (which in 2018 still spent about $40.1bn on space and operated ~1,327 satellites, versus China's ~$5.8bn and ~363). The 'new contenders' story is really a story about access to space diffusing from two Cold-War superpowers to many state and commercial hands.

det_15.title: Scope: what the analyst should build
det_15.claim: Recommended analytical spine, in priority order. (1) The core chart: orbital launches per year by launching state, 1957-2018, with SU+RU merged into one USSR/Russia line, US, China, and Europe ('F'/ESA) as the other leads — this is where the duopoly -> dip -> China-rising arc reads at a glance, and where the 'new contenders' headline lands. (2) Composition over time by agency_type (state vs private vs startup) — show 'startup' appearing only from ~2006 (SpaceX) and the commercial share rising. (3) China's trajectory to the top spot, ending on the 2018 crossover (with the partial-year caveat from det_11 made explicit). (4) Top vehicle families as a texture layer (Soyuz/Kosmos workhorses vs Long March vs Falcon 9) — the agencies.csv lat/long also supports a launch-provider world map. (5) Success-rate by state/era as a reliability check against the det_13 benchmark. Watch-outs: merge SU/RU; label or annualize partial-2018; clean the '2918' typo; recompute counts from launches.csv rather than trusting agencies.csv's 'count' column. The headline finding most defensible from data + context: the launch field has pluralized — the US never collapsed, but it lost its two-way race as China and a new commercial sector turned a duel into a crowd.
